title: Attention Is All You Need (2017): the architecture in detail
text:
CHAPTER 18. TRANSFORMERS
SECTION 18.1. ATTENTION IS ALL YOU NEED (2017): THE ARCHITECTURE IN DETAIL

In June 2017, eight researchers at Google Brain and Google Research, Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser and Illia Polosukhin, posted "Attention Is All You Need" on arXiv (presented at NIPS 2017). It proposed the transformer, a sequence model with no recurrence and no convolution, built entirely from attention (Section 17.3) and simple feedforward layers. It translated better than previous systems at a fraction of the training cost, and its parallel structure fitted GPUs and TPUs so well that it became the basis of BERT, GPT, and nearly every large model through 2026, including models for images, audio, proteins and robot control. This section walks through the architecture piece by piece, with dimensions from the paper's "base" model.

1. Motivation

Recurrent networks (Sections 13.4 and 17.2) compute h_t from h_(t-1), so the positions of a sequence must be processed one after another. During training, this sequential dependency limits parallelism, even on hardware that can do thousands of operations at once. Information between distant words also has to pass through many steps. Convolutional sequence models (such as ByteNet and ConvS2S, 2016-2017) were parallel but needed many layers to connect distant positions. Self-attention connects every pair of positions in one layer and computes all positions in parallel. The paper's comparison table summarized this: per layer, self-attention has O(n^2 d) complexity, O(1) sequential operations and maximum path length O(1); a recurrent layer has O(n d^2) complexity, O(n) sequential operations and path length O(n), where n is the sequence length and d the representation size.

2. Overall structure

The original transformer is an encoder-decoder for translation:

  - The encoder is a stack of N = 6 identical layers. Each has two sublayers: multi-head self-attention, and a position-wise feedforward network.
  - The decoder is a stack of N = 6 layers, each with three sublayers: masked multi-head self-attention over the output generated so far, multi-head cross-attention over the encoder's output, and a feedforward network.
  - Every sublayer is wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)): a residual connection (Section 16.3) followed by layer normalization.
  - All sublayers and embeddings produce vectors of dimension d_model = 512.

The decoder's output goes through a linear layer and a softmax to give probabilities over the vocabulary for the next token.

3. Input: embeddings and positional encoding

Text is split into subword tokens with byte-pair encoding (Section 17.1); for English-German, the paper used a shared source-target vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens. Each token is mapped to a learned 512-dimensional embedding (multiplied by sqrt(d_model)). The input and output embeddings and the pre-softmax linear layer shared the same weight matrix.

Attention by itself is permutation-invariant: shuffling the input words would just shuffle the outputs, so the model has no sense of order. The transformer adds a positional encoding to each embedding. The paper used fixed sinusoids:

    PE(pos, 2i)     = sin( pos / 10000^(2i / d_model) )
    PE(pos, 2i + 1) = cos( pos / 10000^(2i / d_model) )

for position pos and dimension index i. Each pair of dimensions is a sinusoid of a different wavelength, forming a geometric progression from 2 pi to 10000 x 2 pi, like the hands of a clock running at different speeds. For position 1, the first three even dimensions are sin(1), sin(1/10000^(2/512)), sin(1/10000^(4/512)), about 0.841, 0.822 and 0.802. The authors chose sinusoids because, for any fixed offset k, PE(pos + k) is a linear function of PE(pos), which might help the model attend by relative position; learned position embeddings gave nearly identical results. Later models used learned absolute embeddings (GPT, BERT), relative position biases (T5), or rotary position embeddings (RoPE, Jianlin Su and colleagues, 2021), which rotate query and key vectors by position-dependent angles so their dot product depends only on relative distance. RoPE is used in most open large language models in the 2020s.

4. Scaled dot-product attention

As in Section 17.3:

    Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q K^T / sqrt(d_k) ) V

For a sequence of n tokens with queries and keys of dimension d_k, Q K^T is an n x n matrix of scores, each row is normalized by the softmax, and the result multiplies V (n x d_v), giving an n x d_v output. Everything is matrix multiplication plus an element-wise softmax, ideal for GPUs.

5. Multi-head attention

One attention operation computes one weighted average per position, which can only focus on one kind of relationship at a time. Multi-head attention runs h attention operations ("heads") in parallel on different learned projections:

    head_i = Attention( X W_Q^i, X W_K^i, X W_V^i )
    MultiHead(X) = Concat(head_1, ..., head_h) W_O

The base model uses h = 8 heads with d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64, so the total computation is similar to one head with full dimension. Different heads can learn different patterns: some attend to the previous word, some to syntactically related words, some to the matching word in the source sentence. In cross-attention, Q comes from the decoder and K, V from the encoder output.

Parameter count of one attention sublayer: four d_model x d_model matrices (W_Q, W_K, W_V for all heads together, and W_O), so 4 x 512^2 = 1,048,576 weights, about 1.05 million, plus biases.

6. The feedforward sublayer

Each position is then processed independently by the same two-layer network:

    FFN(x) = max(0, x W_1 + b_1) W_2 + b_2

with inner dimension d_ff = 2048 (four times d_model) and ReLU (later models use GELU or gated variants such as SwiGLU). Parameters: 2 x 512 x 2048 = 2,097,152, about 2.1 million, twice as many as the attention sublayer. A common intuition is that attention moves information between positions, while the feedforward layers process information at each position and store much of the model's learned knowledge.

7. Counting parameters

Using the numbers above and ignoring biases and layer norms:

    encoder layer: 1.05M (self-attention) + 2.10M (FFN) = 3.15M
    decoder layer: 1.05M (self) + 1.05M (cross) + 2.10M (FFN) = 4.19M
    6 encoder + 6 decoder layers: 6 x (3.15 + 4.19)M = about 44.0M
    shared embedding: 37,000 x 512 = about 18.9M
    total: about 63M

which matches the paper's reported 65 million parameters for the base model (the difference is biases, normalization parameters and the exact vocabulary size). The "big" model used d_model = 1024, d_ff = 4096 and 16 heads, for 213 million parameters.

8. Masking in the decoder

During training, the decoder receives the whole target sentence, shifted right by one position (with a start token at the beginning), and predicts every next token at once. To keep the prediction at position i from seeing positions after i, the decoder's self-attention uses a causal mask: scores for future positions are set to minus infinity, so their softmax weights are zero. This allows parallel training of all positions while preserving left-to-right generation. At inference time, tokens are still generated one at a time, as in Section 17.2.

9. Training details and results

The paper trained on WMT 2014 English-German (about 4.5 million sentence pairs) and English-French (about 36 million) on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model trained for 100,000 steps, about 12 hours; the big model for 300,000 steps, 3.5 days. Other details:

  - Adam (Section 16.3) with beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.98 and epsilon = 10^-9.
  - A learning rate schedule with warm-up:

        lrate = d_model^(-0.5) x min( step^(-0.5), step x warmup_steps^(-1.5) )

    with warmup_steps = 4000: the rate increases linearly for the first 4,000 steps, then decreases in proportion to the inverse square root of the step number. Warm-up turned out to be important for stable transformer training.
  - Dropout of 0.1 (base) on sublayer outputs and on embeddings plus positional encodings.
  - Label smoothing of 0.1: the target distribution puts 0.9 on the correct token and spreads the rest over the vocabulary, which hurt perplexity but improved accuracy and BLEU.
  - Beam search with beam size 4 and a length penalty, and checkpoint averaging.

Results: the big model reached BLEU 28.4 on English-German, more than 2 BLEU above the best previous results, including ensembles, and 41.8 on English-French, a new single-model state of the art, with training costs a small fraction of those of previous best models. The paper also showed the transformer working on English constituency parsing, a hint that it was a general sequence model.

10. Computational cost

For a sequence of n tokens, the attention scores Q K^T cost about 2 n^2 d multiply-add operations per layer, while the feedforward layers cost about 2 n x 2 d d_ff (forward pass, counting multiplies and adds). For n = 1,000 and d = 512, that is about 1.0 billion operations for the scores versus about 4.2 billion for the FFN, so for short and medium sequences most compute is in the dense matrix multiplications. As n grows, the n^2 term dominates, and memory for the n x n score matrix becomes a limit. This led to many "efficient attention" methods (sparse, local and linear-attention variants) and, most importantly in practice, to FlashAttention (Section 15.2), which computes exact attention in blocks without storing the full matrix.

During generation, the keys and values of past tokens do not change, so they are cached (the "KV cache") rather than recomputed. For long contexts and large batches, this cache dominates memory; multi-query attention (Noam Shazeer, 2019) and grouped-query attention (Joshua Ainslie and colleagues, 2023) share keys and values across heads to shrink it.

11. Variants of the block

Three families grew from the original:

  - Encoder-only (BERT, Section 18.2): bidirectional self-attention, for understanding and classification.
  - Decoder-only (GPT, Section 18.3): causal self-attention only, for generation; this became the dominant design for large language models.
  - Encoder-decoder (T5, BART, translation models).

Common modifications since 2017 include placing layer normalization before each sublayer ("pre-LN": x + Sublayer(LayerNorm(x))), which trains more stably in deep stacks and removes the need for careful warm-up in some settings (Ruibin Xiong and colleagues, 2020); RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm; SwiGLU feedforward layers; rotary embeddings; and mixture-of-experts layers, where each token is routed to a few of many feedforward "experts," so the parameter count can grow without a proportional increase in computation per token (Switch Transformer, 2021, building on Shazeer and colleagues' 2017 sparsely gated mixture-of-experts layer).

The transformer also left language. The Vision Transformer (ViT; Alexey Dosovitskiy and colleagues, 2020) split images into 16 x 16 pixel patches and treated them as tokens, matching or beating convolutional networks when pretrained on enough data. Transformers were applied to speech (Whisper, 2022), protein structure (AlphaFold 2 used attention-based modules), and robot policies.

12. Why it won

  - Parallelism: all positions in a layer are computed together with large matrix multiplications, the operation GPUs and TPUs perform best (Chapter 15).
  - Short paths: any token can directly use information from any other, easing long-range dependencies.
  - Generality: few assumptions about the data; a sequence of tokens can represent text, image patches, audio frames or actions.
  - Scalability: as later work showed (Section 18.3), performance improves predictably as model size, data and compute grow, and the architecture kept training stably at very large sizes.

13. Summary

  - The transformer (Vaswani and colleagues, June 2017) replaced recurrence with multi-head self-attention plus position-wise feedforward layers, residual connections and layer normalization.
  - Base model: 6 + 6 layers, d_model = 512, 8 heads of size 64, d_ff = 2048, about 65 million parameters; big model 213 million.
  - Positional encodings supply word order; causal masking enables parallel training of a left-to-right decoder.
  - Trained with Adam, warm-up, dropout and label smoothing on 8 P100 GPUs: BLEU 28.4 (En-De) and 41.8 (En-Fr), state of the art at low training cost.
  - Attention costs O(n^2) in sequence length; FlashAttention, KV caching, multi-query and grouped-query attention address practical costs.
  - Its encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder variants underlie BERT, GPT, T5, ViT and nearly all large models since.
